questions.question_text:
f(x) = x^3 + 2x^2 - 8x + 5
(a) Find f''(x) (2)
(b) (i) Solve f''(x) = 0 (ii) Hence find the range of values of x for which f(x) is concave. (2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts to differentiate twice: f'(x) = 3x^2 + 4x - 8, then f''(x) = 6x + 4. It can be scored for any correct step in x^3 -> ...x^2 -> ...x or 2x^2 -> ...x -> k or -8x -> k -> 0. A1cso: f''(x) = 6x + 4, the correct second derivative from fully correct work (do not apply isw - mark their final simplified answer). (2 marks)
(b) (i) B1ft: Solves their linear "6x+4" = 0 to get x = -2/3 (follow through on their attempt to differentiate twice in part (a)). (ii) B1ft: Deduces x <= -2/3 (or x < -2/3), i.e. the range of x for which f(x) is concave, following through on their single value of x from part (i). (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
A sequence u1, u2, u3 ... is defined by
u1 = 35
u(n+1) = un + 7cos(nπ/2) - 5(-1)^n
(a) (i) Show that u2 = 40 (ii) Find the value of u3 and the value of u4 (3)
Given that the sequence is periodic with order 4,
(b) (i) write down the value of u5 (ii) find the value of sum from r=1 to 25 of ur (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a)(i) B1*: Correct application of the formula with n = 1, proceeding correctly to an answer of 40 with no errors, e.g. u2 = 35 + 7cos(π/2) - 5(-1)^1 = 35 + 0 + 5 = 40.
(ii) M1: A correct attempt to use the formula to find a value for u3 or u4 - look for n = 2 substituted correctly into the given formula with u2 = 40 (may be implied by u3 = 28), or their calculated u3 used with n = 3 to find u4. A1: Both correct u3 = 28 and u4 = 33. (3 marks)
(b)(i) B1: u5 = 35 (since the sequence repeats every 4 terms, u5 = u1). (ii) M1: Attempts a correct method to find sum_{r=1}^{25} ur, e.g. sum = 6(35+40+"28"+"33") + 35 (using that 25 terms = 6 complete cycles of the 4 values plus one extra term equal to u1). A1: 851 (correct answer with no working scores both marks). (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
Given that
log2(x + 3) + log2(x + 10) = 2 + 2 log2 x
(a) show that
3x^2 - 13x - 30 = 0 (3)
(b) (i) Write down the roots of the equation 3x^2 - 13x - 30 = 0 (ii) Hence state which of the roots in part (b)(i) is not a solution of log2(x + 3) + log2(x + 10) = 2 + 2 log2 x, giving a reason for your answer. (2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Uses one correct log law, e.g. log2(x+3)+log2(x+10) = log2((x+3)(x+10)), or 2 = log2 4, or 2log2 x = log2(x^2) (this mark is independent of any other errors). dM1: Fully correct work leading to a correct equation not containing logs that is not the printed answer, e.g. (x+3)(x+10) = 4x^2 (depends on the first mark; condone a spurious base such as 10 or e as long as the log work is otherwise correct, i.e. they recover base 2). A1*: Obtains 3x^2 - 13x - 30 = 0 with no processing errors. (3 marks)
(b)(i) B1: Both values correct: x = 6, x = -5/3. (ii) B1: Identifies x = -5/3 as the root that is not a solution, with an acceptable explanation, e.g. "x = -5/3 because log2(-5/3) is not real / gives a math error / is undefined" (requires the correct negative root and a valid reason referencing the log of a negative number not being possible). (2 marks)

questions.question_text:
Coffee is poured into a cup. The temperature of the coffee, H °C, t minutes after being poured into the cup is modelled by the equation
H = Ae^(-Bt) + 30
where A and B are constants.
Initially, the temperature of the coffee was 85 °C.
(a) State the value of A. (1)
Initially, the coffee was cooling at a rate of 7.5 °C per minute.
(b) Find a complete equation linking H and t, giving the value of B to 3 decimal places. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: A = 55 (just look for this value; ignore any units given, e.g. 55 °C). (1 mark)
(b) M1: Differentiates to obtain an expression of the form ± ABe^(-Bt), which may have their A already substituted in, so allow ± ABe^(-Bt) or ± "55"Be^(-Bt). M1: Substitutes t = 0 and their A into their dH/dt, sets it equal to -7.5 (a decrease) and proceeds to find a value for B: -B*"55" = -7.5 => B = 3/22 = awrt 0.136. A1cso: H = 55e^(-0.136t) + 30, the correct equation following fully correct work (condone spurious notation such as integral signs or "+c" that don't affect the solution). (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
The curve C has equation y = f(x)
The curve
- passes through the point P(3, -10)
- has a turning point at P
Given that
dy/dx = 2x^3 - 9x^2 + 5x + k
where k is a constant,
(a) show that k = 12 (2)
(b) Hence find the coordinates of the point where C crosses the y-axis. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Substitutes x = 3 completely into the given derivative, sets it equal to 0 (since P is a turning point) and solves for k: 2(3)^3 - 9(3)^2 + 5(3) + k = 0 => k = ... A1*: Obtains k = 12 with no errors and sufficient working shown, e.g. 54 - 81 + 15 + k = 0 => k = 12. (2 marks)
(b) M1: Attempts to integrate the derivative: evidence can be taken from integrating to obtain at least 2 correct terms from 2x^3 -> ...x^4, -9x^2 -> ...x^3, 5x -> ...x^2, 12 -> ...x. dM1: Substitutes x = 3 into their integrated expression (which includes a constant of integration c), sets this equal to -10 (using the point P(3,-10)) and proceeds to find c (depends on the previous method mark). A1: (0, -28) - condone -28 or y = -28, but there must be no other values or points given. (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
Relative to a fixed origin O,
- A is the point with position vector 12i
- B is the point with position vector 16j
- C is the point with position vector (50i + 136j)
- D is the point with position vector (22i + 24j)
(a) Show that AD is parallel to BC. (2)
Points A, B, C and D are used to model the vertices of a running track in the shape of a quadrilateral.
Runners complete one lap by running along all four sides of the track. The lengths of the sides are measured in metres.
Given that a particular runner takes exactly 5 minutes to complete 2 laps,
(b) calculate the average speed of this runner, giving the answer in kilometres per hour. (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts to find both AD = D - A = (10i + 24j) and BC = C - B = (50i + 120j) (may be seen as column vectors; this mark can be scored for at least one correct component of each vector if no method is shown). A1*cso: Correct work showing AD is parallel to BC, e.g. by showing AD = (1/5)BC (or equivalently BC = 5AD), together with a minimal conclusion such as "hence shown" or a tick. (2 marks)
(b) M1: Attempts to use Pythagoras to find at least two of the lengths of the sides AB, BC, CD, DA of the quadrilateral (may be implied by at least 2 correct lengths). A1: At least 2 lengths correct: DA = sqrt(10^2+24^2) = 26, BC = sqrt(50^2+120^2) = 130, AB = sqrt(12^2+16^2) = 20, CD = sqrt(28^2+112^2) = 28*sqrt(17) (awrt 115 m). dM1: Attempts an average speed, having found all 4 lengths, using total distance for 2 laps divided by 5 minutes (there must be some indication of dividing by 5, which may be implied) - ignore any attempt to get the correct units at this stage. A1: awrt 6.99 km/h (units not required, but if given must be correct); an exact answer such as 4.224 + 0.672*sqrt(17) is also acceptable for this mark. (4 marks)

questions.question_text:
In this question you must show all stages of your working. Solutions relying on calculator technology are not acceptable.
A curve has equation
x^3 + 2xy + 3y^2 = 47
(a) Find dy/dx in terms of x and y (4)
The point P(-2, 5) lies on the curve.
(b) Find the equation of the normal to the curve at P, giving your answer in the form ax + by + c = 0, where a, b and c are integers to be found. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts to differentiate x^3 -> ...x^2 and 3y^2 -> ...y(dy/dx), where the ... are constants. B1: Correct application of the product rule on 2xy: 2xy -> 2x(dy/dx) + 2y. M1: A valid attempt to make dy/dx the subject, with exactly 2 different terms in dy/dx coming from 3y^2 and 2xy (i.e. rearranges (...-...)(dy/dx) = ... => dy/dx = ...). A1: dy/dx = -(2y+3x^2)/(2x+6y), oe e.g. dy/dx = (-2y-3x^2)/(2x+6y). (4 marks)
(b) M1: Substitutes x = -2 and y = 5 into their dy/dx expression (must have both x's and y's in dy/dx), correctly placed, to find the gradient of the tangent: -(2(5)+3(-2)^2)/(2(-2)+6(5)) = -22/26 = -11/13. dM1: Attempts to find the equation of the normal using the negative reciprocal of their tangent gradient (13/11) together with x = -2, y = 5: (y-5) = (13/11)(x+2) (depends on the previous method mark). A1: 13x - 11y + 81 = 0, or any integer multiple of this equation. (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
(a) Express 2 cos θ + 8 sin θ in the form R cos(θ - α), where R and α are constants, R > 0 and 0 < α < π/2. Give the exact value of R and give the value of α in radians to 3 decimal places. (3)
The first three terms of an arithmetic sequence are
cos x, cos x + sin x, cos x + 2 sin x, x ≠ nπ
Given that S9 represents the sum of the first 9 terms of this sequence as x varies,
(b) (i) find the exact maximum value of S9 (ii) deduce the smallest positive value of x at which this maximum value of S9 occurs. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: R = sqrt(2^2+8^2) = sqrt(68) = 2*sqrt(17) (must be the exact form; decimal answers score B0 unless the exact value is also seen, then apply isw). M1: Proceeds to a value for α from tan α = 8/2, or cos α = 2/R, sin α = 8/R (may be implied by awrt 1.33 radians or 76 degrees). A1: α = awrt 1.326. (3 marks)
(b)(i) M1: A value of ±4.5 * their R (using the letter R), not embedded in an unresolved expression unless extracted later - since S9 = 9a + 36d = 9cosx + 36sinx = 4.5*(2cosx+8sinx), this scores once they reach 4.5*their R (may be implied by 9*sqrt(17) or awrt 37.1, which may come from a graphical method, or by 9^2+36^2 = ...). A1: 9*sqrt(17), or an exact equivalent such as sqrt(1377) or 4.5*sqrt(68) (isw once a correct answer is seen). (ii) B1ft: awrt 1.33, following through on their α from part (a) (even if in degrees, e.g. 76, however accurate), since the maximum of S9 occurs at x = their α. (3 marks)

questions.question_text:
The curve C has parametric equations
x = t^2 + 6t - 16
y = 6 ln(t + 3), t > -3
(a) Show that a Cartesian equation for C is
y = A ln(x + B), x > -B
where A and B are integers to be found. (3)
The curve C cuts the y-axis at the point P
(b) Show that the equation of the tangent to C at P can be written in the form
ax + by = c ln 5
where a, b and c are integers to be found. (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts to complete the square: x = (t+3)^2 - 25. M1: Rearranges to (t+3)^2 = x+25, and substitutes correctly into the parametric equation for y: y = 6 ln((x+25)^(1/2)) (depends on rearranging correctly first - e.g. t = sqrt(x+25) - 3 substituted directly is M0). A1cso: y = 3 ln(x+25), including brackets, with all stages of working shown and "y =" appearing at some point. (Other valid methods are accepted, e.g. making t the subject of y = 6ln(t+3) first and substituting into x = t^2+6t-16, or using the power law of logs to write y = 6ln(t+3) as 3ln((t+3)^2) and expanding.) (3 marks)
(b) B1ft: Deduces y = 3ln25 (oe e.g. y = 6ln5) by substituting x = 0 into their Cartesian equation (allow follow through on their equation from (a)). M1: Attempts to find dy/dx = 3/(x+25) and substitutes x = 0 (or equivalently finds dy/dx via the parametric chain rule at t = 2, getting dy/dt / dx/dt = 6/(2*2+6) = 3/25). dM1: Attempts the equation of the tangent using their gradient and the point (0, "3ln25"): y - "3ln25" = "3/25"(x - 0) (depends on the previous method mark). A1: 25y - 3x = 150 ln 5, or any integer multiple of this equation in the form ax + by = c ln5. (4 marks)

questions.question_text:
f(x) = (3kx - 18)/((x+4)(x-2))
where k is a positive constant
(a) Express f(x) in partial fractions in terms of k. (3)
(b) Hence find the exact value of k for which
∫ from -3 to 1 of f(x) dx = 21 (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: Correct form for the partial fractions and sets up the corresponding identity: (3kx-18)/((x+4)(x-2)) = A/(x+4) + B/(x-2) => 3kx - 18 = A(x-2) + B(x+4) (may be implied by two equations in A and B if comparing coefficients). M1: Either substitutes x = 2 or x = -4 to find A or B in terms of k, or expands the RHS, collects terms and compares coefficients (may be implied by one correct fraction, numerator and denominator). A1: (2k+3)/(x+4) + (k-3)/(x-2), with no errors - must be the correct partial fractions, not just correct numerators; one correct fraction only scores B0M1A0. (3 marks)
(b) M1: Attempts to integrate ("2k+3")/(x+4) + ("k-3")/(x-2), scoring for either ".../(x+4) -> ...ln(x+4)" or ".../(x-2) -> ...ln(x-2)" (the constants may be in terms of k, condone invisible brackets). A1ft: ("2k+3")ln(x+4) + ("k-3")ln(x-2), following through their partial fraction numerators in terms of k (condone missing brackets if recovered later, e.g. when applying limits). dM1: A full attempt to find k - substitutes in the limits 1 and -3, subtracts either way round, sets the result equal to 21 and solves for k (condone omission of ln(1) or ln(-1) terms; ln(5) or ln(-5) must be seen but may be disregarded after subtraction). A1: k = 21/ln5 - 6, or an exact equivalent such as (21 - 6ln5)/ln5. (4 marks)

questions.question_text:
A tank in the shape of a cuboid is being filled with water (Figure 1). The base of the tank measures 20 m by 10 m and the height of the tank is 5 m. At time t minutes after water started flowing into the tank the height of the water was h m and the volume of water in the tank was V m^3.
In a model of this situation:
- the sides of the tank have negligible thickness
- the rate of change of V is inversely proportional to the square root of h
(a) Show that
dh/dt = λ/sqrt(h)
where λ is a constant. (3)
Given that:
- initially the height of the water in the tank was 1.44 m
- exactly 8 minutes after water started flowing into the tank the height of the water was 3.24 m
(b) use the model to find an equation linking h with t, giving your answer in the form
h^(3/2) = At + B
where A and B are constants to be found. (5)
(c) Hence find the time taken, from when water started flowing into the tank, for the tank to be completely full. (2)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: dV/dh = 200 stated or used (since the base area is 20*10 = 200 m^2, so V = 200h) - may be implied by their chain rule attempt. M1: Requires dV/dt = k/sqrt(h) (k must not just be a plain number) combined with the chain rule dh/dt = (dh/dV)*(dV/dt), correctly placed, i.e. dh/dt = (1/200)*(k/sqrt(h)). A1*: A rigorous argument with all steps shown, simplifying with no errors to dh/dt = λ/sqrt(h) (where λ = k/200; do not allow the same letter to be used for both constants). (3 marks)
(b) M1: Separates the variables and integrates: sqrt(h) dh = λ dt, to obtain an equation of the form ...h^(3/2) = t + c oe (the constant of integration is not needed for this mark). A1: (2/3)h^(3/2) = t (+c) oe. dM1: Substitutes t = 0 and h = 1.44 and attempts to find c (depends on the previous method mark). ddM1: Substitutes t = 8 and h = 3.24 and their c, and attempts to find λ (depends on both previous method marks). A1: Correct equation from correct work: h^(3/2) = 0.513t + 1.728, oe e.g. h^(3/2) = (513/1000)t + (216/125). (5 marks)
(c) M1: Attempts to substitute h = 5 (the height of a full tank) into their equation of the form h^(3/2) = At + B, and solves for t. A1: t = awrt 18.4 minutes, following a correct equation in (b) (units required, e.g. min, mins). (2 marks)
questions.notes: The QP source text for part (a)'s target relation was badly garbled - the square-root symbol over h was lost in OCR, so the raw extraction reads as 'dh/dt = λ/h' with no visible root sign. I reconstructed it as dh/dt = λ/sqrt(h) because this is the only form consistent with the mark scheme's part (b) working, which separates variables as sqrt(h) dh = λ dt and integrates to h^(3/2) = ...t + c - this integration would not arise from dh/dt = λ/h. Flagging for a human check against the original PDF/image to confirm the root sign.

questions.question_text:
The number of subscribers to two different music streaming companies is being monitored (Figure 2). The number of subscribers, NA, in thousands, to company A is modelled by the equation
NA = |t - 3| + 4, t >= 0
where t is the time in years since monitoring began.
The number of subscribers, NB, in thousands, to company B is modelled by the equation
NB = 8 - |2t - 6|, t >= 0
where t is the time in years since monitoring began.
Figure 2 shows a sketch of the graph of NA and the graph of NB over a 5-year period.
Use the equations of the models to answer parts (a), (b), (c) and (d).
(a) Find the initial difference between the number of subscribers to company A and the number of subscribers to company B. (2)
When t = T company A reduced its subscription prices and the number of subscribers increased.
(b) Suggest a value for T, giving a reason for your answer. (2)
(c) Find the range of values of t for which NA > NB giving your answer in set notation. (5)
(d) State a limitation of the model used for company B. (1)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Uses the models to find the difference when t = 0: NA - NB = (3+4) - (8-6) = ... (allow slips in evaluating NA and NB, but it must be clear that t = 0 is being used). A1: 5000 (or 5 thousand) subscribers. (2 marks)
(b) B1: T = 3 (just look for the number 3, so e.g. "t > 3" or "just after 3" is acceptable; must be seen in part (b), not just on the diagram). B1: Any acceptable reason, e.g. "this was the point when company A had the lowest number of subscribers" / "after this point the number of subscribers started to increase" / "it is the minimum/turning point" (allow this mark even if the first B mark was not scored, provided there are no contradictory statements). (2 marks)
(c) B1: Forms one valid equation with the modulus removed, e.g. -t+7 = 2t+2 or t+1 = 14-2t (allow an equation or any inequality sign). M1: Attempts to solve one valid equation. A1: One of the critical values t = 5/3 or t = 13/3 correct. A1ft: Chooses the outside region for their two critical values t = a and t = b (0 < a < b), i.e. t < a, t > b. A1: Fully correct solution in set notation, e.g. {t : t < 5/3} ∪ {t : t > 13/3}. (5 marks)
(d) B1: Any indication that the model is limited because the number of subscribers could become negative for company B, e.g. "it allows negative subscribers (which isn't possible)" or "8 - |2t-6| < 0 for t > 7, so the model isn't valid after t = 7" (not just "subscribers will become zero"). (1 mark)

questions.question_text:
In this question you must show all stages of your working. Solutions relying entirely on calculator technology are not acceptable.
(a) Find the first three terms, in ascending powers of x, of the binomial expansion of
(3 + x)^(-2)
writing each term in simplest form. (4)
(b) Using the answer to part (a) and using algebraic integration, estimate the value of
∫ from 0.2 to 0.4 of 6x/(3+x)^2 dx
giving your answer to 4 significant figures. (4)
(c) Find, using algebraic integration, the exact value of
∫ from 0.2 to 0.4 of 6x/(3+x)^2 dx
giving your answer in the form a ln b + c, where a, b and c are constants to be found. (5)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) M1: Attempts a binomial expansion by taking out a factor of 3^(-2) (or 1/9) and achieves at least the first 3 terms of (1+x/3)^(-2). M1: A correct method to find either the x or the x^2 term unsimplified, e.g. (-2)(kx) or [(-2)(-3)/2!](kx)^2, k ≠ 1. A1: A correct unsimplified or simplified expansion of (1+x/3)^(-2), e.g. 1 + (-2)(x/3) + [(-2)(-3)/2!](x/3)^2. A1: 1/9 - 2x/27 + x^2/27 cao (isw once a correct simplified answer is seen; terms may be listed). (4 marks)
(b) M1: Attempts to multiply their expansion from part (a) by 6x (or just x) and attempts to integrate - look for x^n -> x^(n+1) at least once. A1: Correct integration, simplified or unsimplified: x^2/3 - 4x^3/27 + x^4/18 oe. dM1: An overall problem-solving mark for using part (a) by integrating 6x * their binomial expansion, and substituting in the limits 0.4 and 0.2 and subtracting either way round (may be implied). A1: awrt 0.03304 (exact value 223/6750 = 0.033037...) - isw following a correct answer. (4 marks)
(c) M1: An overall problem-solving mark for using an appropriate integration technique (e.g. substitution u = x+3, integration by parts, or partial fractions), and integrating one of the resulting terms to a natural logarithm, e.g. a/u -> b ln u. M1: Integrates to achieve an expression of the required form for their chosen method, e.g. (using substitution u = x+3) a/u -> b ln u and -a/u^2 -> b/u, giving an antiderivative of the form ...ln u + .../u. A1: Correct integration for their method, e.g. 6ln u + 18/u (substitution, u = x+3), or equivalently 6ln(3+x) + 18/(3+x) (partial fractions: 6x/(3+x)^2 = 6/(3+x) - 18/(3+x)^2), or 6ln(3+x) - 6x/(3+x) (integration by parts) - all equivalent up to a constant. ddM1: Substitutes in the correct limits (0.4 and 0.2, or the corresponding changed limits 3.4 and 3.2 if using substitution) for their integral and subtracts either way round to find a value (depends on both previous method marks). A1: 6 ln(17/16) - 45/136 (a full and rigorous argument leading to this exact value, or an exact equivalent such as 3 ln(289/256) - 45/136; the ln term must be exact). (5 marks)

questions.question_text:
In this question you must show all stages of your working. Solutions relying entirely on calculator technology are not acceptable.
(a) Show that the equation
2 tan θ (8 cos θ + 23 sin^2 θ) = 8 sin 2θ (1 + tan^2 θ)
may be written as
sin 2θ (A cos^2 θ + B cos θ + C) = 0
where A, B and C are constants to be found. (3)
(b) Hence, solve for 360° <= x <= 540°
2 tan x (8 cos x + 23 sin^2 x) = 8 sin 2x (1 + tan^2 x)
x ≠ 450° (4)
questions.mark_scheme_text:
(a) B1: For recalling and using at least one correct trigonometric identity in the given equation, e.g. sin^2θ + cos^2θ = 1, 1 + tan^2θ = sec^2θ, tanθ = sinθ/cosθ, or sin2θ = 2sinθcosθ (may be seen explicitly or implied by their working). M1: For manipulating the equation using trig identities (condoning sign slips only in the identities and arithmetic slips) to obtain an expression of the form A sin2θ cos^2θ + B sin2θ cosθ + C sin2θ (= 0), or sin2θ(A cos^2θ + B cosθ + C) (= 0), with A, B, C ≠ 0. A1: sin2θ(23cos^2θ - 8cosθ - 15) = 0 oe (i.e. A = 23, B = -8, C = -15), cao (the "= 0" is not required for the M1 but is required for the A1). (3 marks)
(b) B1: One of x = 360° or x = 540° (from sin2x = 0; the degree symbol is not required; may come from cosx = 1). M1: Attempts to solve their 3-term quadratic 23cos^2x - 8cosx - 15 = 0 (or a "made up" 3TQ), leading to a value for cosx (allow a calculator solution, may be implied by at least one correct value). dM1: Attempts to find one of their angles in the range 360 <= x <= 540 (but not 450) for their cosx = k, k ≠ 1 (must be checked, e.g. cos(their x) = their k). A1: x = 360, 540 and awrt 491 only, with no other values in range (including 450) - awrt 491 must come from cosx = -15/23. (4 marks)

questions.question_text:
A student attempts to answer the following question:
Given that x is an obtuse angle, use algebra to prove by contradiction that
sin x - cos x >= 1
The student starts the proof with:
Assume that sin x - cos x < 1 when x is an obtuse angle
=> (sin x - cos x)^2 < 1
=> ...
The start of the student's proof is reprinted below. Complete the proof. (3)
questions.mark_scheme_text: M1: Expands (sinx - cosx)^2 to obtain sin^2x ∓ 2sinx cosx + cos^2x < 1 (i.e. sin^2x - 2sinx cosx + cos^2x < 1), may be implied. A1: Uses the identity sin^2x + cos^2x = 1 to obtain a correct inequality in any form that does not include the sin^2x and cos^2x terms, e.g. 1 - 2sinx cosx < 1, i.e. -2sinx cosx < 0 (or equivalently -sin2x < 0). A1*: Fully correct work which includes: a convincing argument that explains why the inequality is not true (e.g. "as x is obtuse, sinx > 0 and cosx < 0, so -2sinx cosx is positive, but we need -2sinx cosx < 0"), a statement that indicates there is a contradiction, and a conclusion that sinx - cosx >= 1 (no need to repeat "when x is obtuse"; no contradictory or mixed-variable statements). (3 marks)
